summary.text: An electric field is a physical field surrounding charged particles such as electrons, describing their ability to push or pull on other charges.
At any point it is defined as the force a small positive test charge would feel there, divided by that charge, so it has a direction as well as a size.
A bigger charge makes a stronger field, and the field of a single charge weakens the farther you move from it.

facts.label: Unit
facts.value: Volts per metre, equal to newtons per coulomb

facts.label: Where it comes from
facts.value: Electric charges and time-varying electric currents

facts.label: Field lines
facts.value: A drawing idea introduced by Michael Faraday

facts.label: Distance rule
facts.value: Twice as far away means a quarter of the strength

facts.label: Line density
facts.value: Closer-packed lines show a stronger field

items.prompt: You stand near a charged balloon and then step back until you are twice as far away. How strong is its field where you stand now?

options.label: One quarter of what it was
Half of what it was
The same, since the balloon is unchanged
Twice what it was

items.explain: The field of a point charge falls with the square of the distance, so twice as far gives a quarter.

items.prompt: You charge a balloon more heavily by rubbing it for longer. What happens to the field close to it?

options.label: It weakens, as the extra charge spreads out
It gets stronger as the charge grows
It stays put, because the field depends on distance only
It disappears once the balloon holds too much

items.explain: The greater the charge of an object, the stronger its electric field.

items.prompt: In a drawing of field lines, one region has lines packed tightly and another has them spread far apart. What does that show?

options.label: The field is weak where lines are packed tight
The field is zero where lines are far apart
The field is strong where lines are packed tight
The two regions hold opposite kinds of charge

items.explain: Lines are drawn so that their density is proportional to the strength of the field.

items.prompt: Following a field line drawn around fixed charges, where does it start and where does it end?

options.label: It starts on negative charges and ends on positive ones
It starts and ends on the same charge
It starts and ends on neutral objects
It starts on positive charges and ends on negative ones

items.explain: Field lines of stationary charges begin at positive charges (or infinity) and end at negative charges (or infinity).

items.prompt: A field is measured with a tiny probe charge. Why do we divide the probe's force by its charge?

options.label: So the result describes the field, not the probe used
So the probe's own charge can be ignored for safety
So that the answer always comes out as a whole number
So the force no longer needs a direction attached

items.explain: The field is defined as force per unit of charge on a small positive test charge, which makes it a property of the surroundings.

items.prompt: A diagram shows field lines around a charge with empty gaps between the lines. What is in those gaps?

options.label: Nothing, so a charge placed there feels no force
A weaker field that is only half the line value
A field of the opposite sign to the lines
The field too, since it fills all the space

items.explain: The lines are a way of drawing the field; the field itself fills all the space between them.
